items.text: The previous turn made concrete progress, but left the main theorem open. I’m now testing a different mechanism: whether a fixed nonlinear activation can keep a positive fraction of first-layer features exactly unchanged during training, and whether that supplies the missing global control.

The plateau activation gives a useful new foothold: some first-layer features stay fixed under the actual training dynamics. I’m checking whether this prevents the concentration problem that remains open, including whether second-layer features can retain enough variation throughout training.

items.text: The new mechanism appears to preserve a positive readout kernel on each finite time interval. That would be useful, but it does not yet establish the joint limit: the proof still needs to control the backward fields generated by repeated use of the same Gaussian matrix. I’m testing that missing implication directly.

A second useful bound is now derived: for the plateau activation, first-layer weights cannot drift arbitrarily far, even under arbitrary integrable driving signals. The proof covers singular input Grams. I’m checking it independently; it controls weight amplitudes, while the backward-field and finite-width limits remain separate obligations.

The sharper kernel estimate still does not close the argument. For the moderate plateau activation, its guaranteed lower bound decays too quickly to prove a finite residual clock. I have also derived compactness estimates for several bounded feature-path laws; the raw backward fields and the first-layer kernel remain outside those estimates.

I’m testing two further ways to control the remaining term: a time-ordered expansion for a bounded sine activation, and a comparison estimate that includes the backward fields themselves. Both retain the original Gaussian initialization and training equations. The key question is whether they can prevent concentration without assuming the tail bound we need to prove.

An isolated reviewer accepted the confinement argument but found a missing regularity condition in its population corollary. I’ve added it explicitly and sent the complete corrected report to a fresh reviewer. This review concerns only the confinement lemma; the global joint-limit theorem is still open.

items.text: The proof attempts confirm that the single trained Gaussian matrix still creates feedback between the two layers. Removing one neuron has a vanishing effect on the bulk state, yet leaves an order-one return in that neuron’s own field. Any valid limit must retain that return. I’m using this calculation to rule out an overly simple independence argument and focus the estimates on the actual coupled dynamics.

The new approximation preserves the original loss dissipation and gives bounds independent of the cutoff. The remaining gap is removing that cutoff: energy bounds alone do not rule out concentration in the backward fields. I’m testing whether the dynamics provide the additional control needed.

items.text: There is now a rigorous positive special case: for orthogonal inputs, certain bounded nonlinear activations admit global population flows through an exact change of coordinates. Correlated inputs prevent that same cancellation, so this does not settle your target. I’m consolidating the approximation and continuation lemmas for isolated review while testing a cancellation that couples both layers.

The approximation and conditional continuation proof has passed one fresh isolated review; a second is still checking it. The tail estimate needed to make it unconditional remains open. A new Gaussian projection estimate controls part of the feedback more directly, and I’m testing whether it closes that gap.

Both fresh isolated reviewers passed the partial manuscript without objections. The unconditional result is the dissipative approximation; continuation still depends on an unproved tail estimate. The Gaussian projection route also remains unclosed: a component omitted by the projection can affect the next Gaussian field, so I cannot discard it.

**The full \(L=2\) result remains unresolved.** I have neither a complete proof nor a counterexample to the actual training dynamics.

I proved global, energy-dissipating approximations and a **conditional** continuation theorem. Two fresh isolated adversarial reviewers passed that manuscript without objections.

The missing step is proving sufficient concentration control for the actual backward fields. Energy bounds and Gaussian projection estimates do not supply it; the finite-width GF/GD identification also remains required.

The [current report](/home/amir/Codes/PDE/studies/mean_field_peeling/practical_fixed_depth2/RESULT.md) records the precise results and gaps. The research goal remains active—these partial reviews do not certify the theorem you requested.

items.text:
The earlier proof uses separation mainly to guarantee fast fitting and keep the entire trajectory under control. Your compact-time limit target may avoid that requirement. Also, the latest gain-based result already improves the dependence on separation to a polynomial, but its numerical constants still make the relative nonlinearity tiny.

The depth idea has a separate subtlety: a near-identity activation followed by a fresh Gaussian matrix is not a near-identity layer. The random mixing can prevent small nonlinear effects from accumulating in the way they do in a residual network.

I found a more precise version of your depth idea. For the original Gaussian-layer model, changes in normalized feature geometry start at the square of the activation perturbation. That suggests \(1/\sqrt L\), with variance calibration, as a better candidate than \(1/L\). For genuine residual layers, coherent \(1/L\) accumulation does work.

My recommendation is to tackle compact-time continuation at fixed depth first, using a fixed, moderately nonlinear activation. That targets the main missing theorem directly; the corrected depth construction is a promising second route.

The proposed next theorem would keep the activation fixed as \(T\) grows and allow the proof’s bounds to depend on \(T\). That avoids turning “global” into a requirement for uniformly fast fitting.

I’ve written up the comparison, including an explicit variance-calibrated \(1/\sqrt L\) activation. Independent readers are checking the new initialization calculations and making sure they support only the proposed research direction, without implying a trained-network theorem.

items.text: The assessment also separates “provably nonzero” from “practically substantial” nonlinearity. A positive absolute regression gap can coexist with an overwhelming affine contribution. For the depth route, the useful requirement is a nonlinear effect that remains visible after normalizing the final features, even as each layer’s perturbation vanishes.

items.text:
**Yes. You want the nonlinear effect of the whole network to remain substantial, while preserving global population existence and the joint finite-width limit on every compact training interval.** Infinitely small nonlinearities could serve that purpose if their cumulative effect survives.

My recommendation is to **prioritize a new fixed-depth continuation argument, starting at \(L=2\)**. I would keep the depth idea as a second direction, with a different scaling from the one we initially considered.

The crucial change is your clarification of the target. We need one fixed activation for which the theorem holds on every \([0,T]\); the estimates may depend on \(T\). We do not need uniformly fast fitting, an all-time positive kernel floor, or a finite total residual clock. The earlier proof obtained those stronger properties together, and this drove its restrictive activation choice.

Indeed, true finite-width GF already satisfies
\[
\int_0^T\|\dot\Theta_n(t)\|_{\rm raw}^{2}\,dt
\le \mathcal E_n(0),
\qquad
\sup_{t\le T}\|\Theta_n(t)-\Theta_n(0)\|_{\rm raw}
\le\sqrt{T\mathcal E_n(0)}.
\]
Neither estimate uses input separation or a tiny nonlinear coefficient.

**The remaining difficulty is passing this control to the canonical population flow and identifying the joint limit.** Energy alone does not give strong compactness in the infinite-dimensional state space. The backward fields also create a genuine stability problem through terms such as \(\psi''(z)q\). Previous energy-only approaches did not close that gap.

So I would target a compact-time estimate for the *actual physical trajectories*: sufficient control of backward-field tails, or a direct stability estimate that avoids requiring those tails. Crucially, its constants may deteriorate with \(T\), while the activation stays fixed. A concrete research target would be your convex family with, say, \(\varepsilon=1/4\) and \(\psi=\tanh\). **That is a proposed target, not an established theorem.**

There is also a correction to the quantitative picture: the latest gain-based construction already has polynomial separation dependence—relative amplitude \(e/a\) behaves like \(\delta^2\) for fixed shape. Its enormous numerical constants still make it practically near affine. Thus changing “exponential” to “polynomial” alone would not resolve your concern.

Your depth intuition is sound, but there are two different mechanisms.

For genuinely residual layers,
\[
h_{\ell+1}=h_\ell+\frac{\beta}{L}F(h_\ell),
\]
small nonlinear effects can accumulate coherently. For example, taking \(F=\tanh\), the continuous-depth map is
\[
h(1)=\operatorname{arsinh}\!\bigl(e^\beta\sinh h(0)\bigr),
\]
which is nonlinear even though each discrete layer approaches identity.

But our original layer is
\[
h_{\ell+1}=\phi_L(W_{\ell+1}h_\ell).
\]
A fresh Gaussian matrix remains between activations. This changes the accumulation mechanism.

I checked an exact initialization calculation: for \(\phi_\varepsilon(z)=z+\varepsilon\psi(z)\), **the first-order effect changes the common feature scale; changes in normalized feature geometry begin at order \(\varepsilon^2\)**. With controlled variances, choosing \(\varepsilon=\beta/L\) therefore produces only \(O(1/L)\) cumulative new geometry. This is an initialization statement, not a claim that later training must remain linear.

That suggests a more promising Gaussian-network construction: **\(1/\sqrt L\) perturbations, with variance calibration**. One explicit candidate is
\[
r(z)=\arctan z-a_0z,\quad
a_0=\mathbb E[G\arctan G],\quad v=\mathbb E[r(G)^2],
\]
\[
\phi_L(z)=
\frac{z+\beta L^{-1/2}r(z)}
{\sqrt{1+\beta^2v/L}}.
\]
Its initialized variance stays exactly one, and its normalized correlations have a nontrivial nonlinear continuous-depth limit. Thus there is a concrete way to realize your cumulative-nonlinearity idea at initialization. This is a new activation family; it does **not** yet have the global trained theorem.

A genuine residual route is also attractive, but requires specifying the training normalization alongside the architecture. A \(1/L\) residual factor can suppress branch training under an unchanged parameter metric. Relevant [ResNet mean-field work](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume23/21-0669/21-0669.pdf) uses explicitly scaled training dynamics, so its results cannot simply be transferred to our model.

I would therefore pursue:

1. **Fixed \(L=2\):** a fixed, moderately nonlinear activation and compact-time continuation using physical GF structure.
2. **Then \(L=3\):** extend the successful mechanism, without first demanding fast fitting.
3. **Depth:** investigate the calibrated \(1/\sqrt L\) Gaussian construction, or an explicitly specified residual architecture, with end-to-end nonlinearity and training scaling included in the target.

The [detailed assessment and derivations](/home/amir/Codes/PDE/studies/mean_field_peeling/practical_global_limit_assessment/ASSESSMENT.md) passed two fresh isolated adversarial reviews. Those reviews validate the assessment and initialization calculations; the proposed global trained results remain open.
